title: The hidden life (CCC 531–534)
hook: most of Jesus's life was ordinary work in Nazareth

segments.voice: Yesterday, born of the Virgin: Mary's practical question, and her answer, be it done to me. Your line was by the holy spirit. Did a bell remind you? Day one thousand seventy-five.

"Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" That's the hometown crowd in Mark's Gospel, and they aren't impressed. Jesus has come back to his own country and is teaching in the synagogue, and the people who watched him grow up can't square it. They know his mother. They know his brothers by name. They know him as the carpenter. Where did he get all this? Their question is accidentally a window. Before the crowds and the miracles, there were years of something so ordinary that the neighbors remembered him mostly as a tradesman. The Catechism has a name for those years, and it's today's word.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `THE NEIGHBORS CAN'T SQUARE IT.` → `YEARS NOBODY WROTE DOWN.`

segments.voice: The hidden life. The Catechism says that for the greater part of his life, Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of people: a daily life without evident greatness, a life of manual work, the religious life of his people, life in a community. Not a training montage. Just days. The Gospels are nearly silent about them. The Catechism calls the finding in the temple the one event that breaks that silence. Luke tells it: when Jesus was twelve, his family went up to Jerusalem for the feast, and on the way home his parents realized he wasn't with them. After three days they found him in the temple, among the teachers, listening and asking questions. And then comes the line that closes the door on the hidden years again. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." Luke adds one more sentence: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." That's it. Back to the workshop, the family table, the synagogue on the sabbath. The Catechism sees in his obedience to Mary and Joseph a picture of his obedience to the Father. And it draws out something for everyone else. Because of Nazareth, it says, anyone can share in Jesus's life through the most ordinary events of their own day. It quotes Pope Paul the Sixth, speaking at Nazareth, who called it a school: a lesson in silence, in family life, in work. So the plain parts of a life aren't a waiting room before the real thing starts. In Catholic teaching, God made flesh spent most of his years on them.
screen: `THE GREATER PART: PLAIN DAYS.` · `THE GOSPELS ARE NEARLY SILENT.` · `HE WENT DOWN TO NAZARETH.` · `A SCHOOL OF SILENCE, FAMILY, WORK.` · then, large: `AND WAS SUBJECT TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do plain work with love. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the plainest job waiting for you today. Dishes. Emails. A diaper. A shift. A form to fill in. Don't try to make it meaningful. Just see yourself doing it, carefully, as if the person it serves were in the room. Notice your hands, and the pace you'd like to go at. If you pray, you can offer that one task to God before you start it. If you don't, simply choose the person you're doing it for. The bell holds the time.
The hidden life. Jesus's years in Nazareth: work, family, prayer, with almost nothing written down, which the Catechism calls a school for everyone's ordinary days. Today's word.
Your line: nazareth counts. Today, do that one plain job slowly and well, and let nobody know you did it on purpose. Day one thousand seventy-five.

howItsDone: Catholics honor the hidden life at Nazareth on the feast of the Holy Family and in the rosary's joyful mysteries, which end with the finding of Jesus in the temple.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Mark 6:3 (first clause), Luke 2:51 and Luke 2:52.
'The greater part of his life' and 'the vast majority' are CCC 531's own words (paraphrased); 'the one event that breaks that silence' paraphrases CCC 534 ('the only event'). Confirm.
Age twelve and 'after three days' are from Luke 2:42, 46.
Paul VI's Nazareth address (lessons of silence, family life, work) paraphrased from CCC 533; the date is left out under the claims rule.
'The God who took flesh spent most of that flesh's time on them' restates CCC 531 in plain words; Keeper may prefer a softer line.
howItsDone names the feast of the Holy Family and the joyful mysteries ending with the finding in the temple; confirm.
Editor: cut the invented detail that he made the neighbors' tables and doors; 'relatives' tightened to the brothers Mark names.
Audit: Mark 6:1 says 'his own country', not Nazareth by name, so the hook now follows Mark; rewrote the garbled closing line of the teach. Mark 6:3 and Luke 2:51–52 Challoner wording checked.
